Source. `psl_load_fp()` reads the attacker-controlled PoC bytes into `buf` as the first line of a text PSL file. For this witness, that line is the entire 62-byte UTF-8 rule `ڸoa.Dڸ88.ڸoa.ڸ88.Dڸo8.ڸoa.Dڸ88.Dڸ888.Dڸ.Dڸo88.Dڸo88`.

The loader materializes the rule into parser state here. The copied string is still 62 bytes long and contains 11 labels, so the later per-label punycode loop will eventually process final label `Dڸo88` with ten already-emitted predecessors.
The copied rule is not pure ASCII because every label contains UTF-8 bytes `da b8` for `ڸ`, so the early return is skipped and the rule enters punycode conversion.

The staged build executes the fallback branch with a fixed 128-byte stack destination. The saved ASan frame reports this exact `lookupname` object as the overflowed buffer, so every later `outlen` calculation is bounded by 128 bytes.

Before the crashing iteration, the first 10 labels are emitted successfully into `lookupname`. Using the in-tree punycode encoder, those 10 ACE labels plus their 10 dots occupy 116 bytes, so the final label starts with only 12 buffer bytes left.

For the last label `Dڸo88`, `mem_is_ascii(label, labellen)` is false and the non-ASCII branch is taken. Its UTF-8 length is only 6, so the pre-check still passes at `outlen = 116`: `116 + 6 + 0 + 4 = 126 < 128`. The function therefore proceeds into punycode encoding even though the final ACE form plus terminator will need 13 bytes.

Root cause. After copying the `xn--` prefix for the final label, `outlen` becomes 120. This statement then sets `labellen = 8`, exposing all remaining bytes to `punycode_encode()` and leaving no reserved slot for the trailing `out[outlen] = 0`.

`punycode_encode()` emits the final label's 8-byte ACE tail `Do88-qrg` into bytes 120..127 of `lookupname`. Because `labellen` was allowed to consume all remaining space, `outlen` becomes exactly 128 after this increment.

Sink. There is no dot on the final label, so `outlen` is still 128 here and the terminator write targets `lookupname[128]`, one byte beyond the 0..127 stack array. This is the exact 1-byte ASan stack-buffer-overflow WRITE reported in the saved trace.
